They launched it in April, they tightened it in October, and the write-off landed in September.
In April they launched a new product.
Revenue rose in May, and the team read the dashboard every day.
They did not argue about the model.
Did anybody write down the reason?
We launched the product in April, and revenue rose in May and in June.
In August a spike appeared in the default rate, and it did not fall back.
We did not change the model. We read the policy line by line.
Did anybody write down the reason for that change?
We tightened the policy in October, we lost some growth, and we kept the habit.

I have told this story in three companies now, and it lands the same way every time. We launched the product in April and revenue rose in May. It rose again in June. Everybody was happy, and nobody asked a single question, including me. Then in August I saw the default rate climb, and the first thing I did was open the policy, not the model. That surprised my own team. But a model does what the rule tells it to do, and the rule had changed in March. Somebody had loosened it to let more customers in before the end of the quarter. I do not regret the launch. The product was right and it is still running today. What I regret is that nobody wrote down the reason for that change, so it took us three weeks to find something that should have taken ten minutes.

When a company calls me after a bad quarter, I ask two questions in the first ten minutes. Who changed the rule, and why. Almost everybody can answer the first half. Almost nobody can answer the second. And the change is never dramatic, that is the thing. Nobody wakes up and decides to take a huge risk. What happens is small: a team lets in customers with a shorter credit history, because the target for that quarter is close and this gets them there. It looks like nothing on the day it happens. Nine months later it is the whole story. So my advice is boring, and it works. Every change carries three things: a name, a date and a reason. Not a document, not a committee. Three lines, written by the person who made the call, on the day they made it.
